newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan corruption long a way of life.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan corruption long a way of life.

text.p: Corruption is a fact of life in Kenya from the policeman taking a small bribe at a checkpoint to rich businessmen with powerful links and access to millions of dollars.
But what angered the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was the repeated failure of President Daniel arap Moi's government to crack down convincingly on graft and meet its demands for a clean up.
The IMF suspended a key aid programme to Kenya on Thursday, damaging Kenya's international credibility and forcing the government to struggle to cover some of the shortfall of $215 million this year.
But every year, Kenya's auditor-general lists huge amounts of misappropriated government money. Kenya's attorney -general has not successfully prosecuted anyone, citing insufficient evidence.
Western donors say corruption is their major complaint against the government of Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years.
They estimate losses from mismanagement and corruption were greater than aid donations in 1992 and 1993, which the U.N. Development Programme put at $997 million and $857 million respectively.

In 1996, the Berlin-based anti-corruption group Transparency International listed Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan as countries seen by the international business community as the most corrupt places to do business in some 54 countries worldwide.
The listing enraged the government but to this day the courts have failed to identify and to punish those involved in Kenya's biggest single financial scandal, known as Goldenberg.
In 1991 and 1992 the government paid some $100 million to Goldenberg International under a gold and diamond export compensation scheme. The problem was Kenya produces little gold and no diamonds.
Under pressure, authorities charged Goldenberg owner Kamlesh Pattni and four former senior government officials but after four years of delay the high court in June ended their prosecution.

Attorney-General Amos Wako has charged the suspects again but it was too little, too late to convince donors that the opposition was wrong to suspect they were being handled lightly because they could name corrupt officials high in government.
"What donors want are practical steps in dealing with the Goldenburg culprits, no window dressing," said one diplomat.
He said the IMF sought "maximum and strong actions that would send clear strong signals to the public that officials who engage in irregularities could indeed expect certain punitive action".
The IMF was also angered by repeated scandals in Kenya's energy, customs and agriculture sectors that led to huge losses while economic reforms had helped to secure continued aid.

Officials said the IMF was especially concerned by the sudden transfer last month of Samuel Chebii from the post of commissioner of customs and excise even as the IMF was pressing the government hard for a concrete crackdown on corruption.
Chebii, an accountant who was investigating the importation of sugar by companies with links to politicians, was moved to the ministry of finance, where officials said he would continue his clean-up.

But the opposition charged he was silenced as he was close to uncovering which officials had cooperated with sugar imports which were ostensibly only in transit but were diverted on to the Kenyan market.
Corruption is particularly disturbing in a country where unemployment is running at 11 million and still rising and about half of Kenya's 29 million people live below the poverty line.
In 1995, the government temporarily withdrew its official registration of a Kenyan private group that had published a comprehensive report on corruption and demanded firm action.
